description:
Somos el Equipo 2 de Astrochikis Club. Tenemos entre 8 y 10 años y venimos de Ciudad Bolívar, Bogotá.

Somos curiosos, nos gusta investigar, conversar, hacer experimentos y buscar respuestas a las preguntas que tenemos sobre el universo.

En Astrochikis Club hemos aprendido que investigar no es solamente encontrar respuestas, sino también hacernos nuevas preguntas, escuchar las ideas de los demás y trabajar en equipo.

Participamos en NASA Space Apps Cachipay 2026 porque queremos poner a prueba nuestra creatividad, resolver desafíos y compartir lo que sabemos.

¡Porque los niños y las niñas también podemos hacer ciencia y aportar ideas para explorar el universo!
summary:
Four children, ages 8 to 10, from Astrochikis Club designed and built a model of an underground lunar shelter to answer two important questions: How could we breathe and grow food on the Moon?
Their design features three connected levels. The upper level is dedicated to sleeping and storing spacesuits. The middle level is designed for growing food and researching how plants grow and reproduce. The lower level includes bathrooms and showers.
The children also imagined a machine called "The Purifier 3000," designed to help produce oxygen and remove carbon dioxide from the air. They included systems for collecting and reusing water, connecting pipes, and solar panels with a cable that would supply electricity to the shelter.
The project brings together different survival needs and shows how the children used their scientific knowledge to develop their own creative solutions.
details:
What Problem Are We Trying to Solve?

This is an adaptation of the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. The children wondered how humans could live beneath the Moon's surface, where there is no breathable air and special systems would be needed to obtain water, grow food, and provide energy.

To explore this question, they imagined an underground shelter, which they also called an "intralunar shelter" to describe its location beneath the lunar surface.

How Is Our Lunar Shelter Organized?

The children designed three levels, each serving a specific purpose.

Upper Level — Rest and Everyday Life

This level includes beds and storage areas for spacesuits. It was designed as a place where astronauts could rest and carry out their daily activities.

Middle Level — Food Production and Scientific Research

This is one of the most important parts of the project. The children explained that their garden would do more than just produce food.

It would also serve as a laboratory where astronauts could study how plants grow and reproduce, investigate which species might adapt best to the conditions inside a lunar shelter, and explore which foods could be grown there.

To make this possible, plants would need water, nutrients, proper lighting, and suitable environmental conditions.

Lower Level — Hygiene and Water Recycling

The children placed bathrooms and showers on this level.

They connected this area to their idea of collecting, treating, and reusing water to avoid wasting a resource that would be essential for living beyond Earth.

How Would the Oxygen System Work?

The children created a concept called "The Purifier 3000," represented by a machine connected to a network of pipes.

Their goal was to address two essential challenges: providing oxygen for astronauts to breathe and removing the carbon dioxide they exhale.

To develop their idea, they explored how water is recovered and purified on space stations, how oxygen can be produced through water electrolysis, and why excess carbon dioxide must be removed from the air.

In real spacecraft, producing oxygen and removing carbon dioxide require specific processes and equipment.

The Purifier 3000 is the children's conceptual design for bringing these essential functions together. It is not a working machine, and its performance has not been tested.

Where Would the Energy Come From?

The children proposed using solar panels installed on the Moon's surface.

On their model, they added a white connection at the back to represent an electrical cable carrying power from the solar panels to the machines and different areas inside the shelter.

How Did We Develop Our Project?

The children began by identifying two basic needs: breathing and eating.

They then explored possible solutions through short videos, scientific resources, and guided discussions based on their own questions.

They created drawings, discussed ideas, selected materials, and built a three-level model using boxes, cardboard, pipes, and other simple materials.

As the project developed, they added new ideas about water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, growing food, and energy.

What Makes Our Solution Creative?

The children did not simply design separate rooms. They created a shelter where food production, rest, hygiene, water, air, and energy are all connected.

They also turned their garden into a scientific research space and invented their own machine, The Purifier 3000, to address the challenges of providing breathable air.

Why Is This Project Important?

This project shows how children can identify real challenges in space exploration, investigate possible solutions, and work together to develop their own design.

One of their most important discoveries was understanding that living on the Moon is not just about having the right objects or equipment. It requires designing systems that work together to solve different survival challenges.

The final result is an educational concept model, not a habitable lunar shelter or a functioning life-support system.
